utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Konings, I would like to remind that you the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony is still binding you. Mr. Russo, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I am Mr. President. Thank you. I'd like to begin, Mr. Registrar, please, with Exhibit P1259 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, I'd like to begin your discussion today with regard to some of the principles you set forth in your expert report with respect to targeting and, in particular, the planning of artillery operations in civilian-populated areas. And if we could turn to section 4 of your expert report. Again, that's at tab 2 of your binder, Colonel Konings. Section 4 appears at the bottom of page 4 of the English version and on page 10 in the B/C/S version. Now, in this section, Colonel Konings, you discuss the considerations that go into artillery targeting in civilian-populated areas and at sub-section a, you state: "On the basis of the higher commanders intention and guidelines and the results of the decision-making process, DMP, the high pay-off, HPT targets are identified by the commander." Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what exactly you mean by a high pay-off target?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A high pay-off target is a target that is crucial for the positive outcome of your own operation. So combatting that target with a certain effect that you want to achieve is crucial for the success, as I said, of your own operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does the mere fact that a commander identifies a particular target as a high pay-off target does that automatically mean that it is appropriate to fire artillery at it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At this stage that -- that this all is planned, it is just a matter of designating a target that it has a very high value for your own operation. And those high pay-off targets are coming from the so-called high-value target list which are those targets that are very interesting or very crucial for the operation of the enemy. And only in a later stage once you have designed those high pay-off targets you start working on the process of choosing the appropriate weapon systems for bringing the effect that you want to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the decision-making process and the selection of high pay-off targets that you discuss, can you tell Chamber whether this process happens at the highest operational level or at some other levels, in general?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- a decision-making process takes place at every command level inside -- inside a military organisation. That runs from the strategic level, the very high level, which is connected to the political level, down to the tactical level. Also, a commander of a company or even a platoon commander has his own decision-making process although that is very quick and it's -- it's only -- it's not formalised it's not in a way of written down. But on the level of divisions, brigades and battalions, have you a decision-making process and all those levels you also have a targeting process. From brigade level and above, the targeting process is getting more formal, so it is a formalised process in which -- which is done in formal and informal meetings inside a staff. On battalion level and lower, you only have a very quick and informal targeting process, but the outcome is nevertheless the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if a high pay-off target which is identified by a commander is located in a civilian-populated area can you please explain to the Chamber what the commander has to consider before deciding to attack that particular high pay-off target with artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, even before you take the decision to attack such a target which is in the middle of the civilian-populated area, you have to be absolutely sure that the value of that target for your own operation is such -- is such that combatting a target with any weapon systems is proportionate and that the risk that you take for collateral damage will be -- well, in words like acceptable. And that's very often a very high-level decision. That is, not on the level of a brigade commander's decision at least not in the NATO case. So after you have designated that the target is absolutely a very valuable target you have to see what is the nature that the target is, is it in a concrete building; is it in a command post; is it in -- which kind of terrain is it; what are the elements of such a target; is it a large target; is it a small target; how is the best way to -- to put an effect on at that target; do you neat to destroy it completely to take it out; to take it out of action or is neutralising; taking it temporarily out of action; is that sufficient for the purpose that you have; so you have to discuss the effect you want to achieve. Very important is, of course, how close is the civilian population; how is construction of that area; how is the infrastructure laid out. That is the one of the most important points to decide upon which weapon system you can use, and, of course, you can use every weapon system, but then you have to realise that once you start using artillery in a civilian-populated area that you will have to -- a high risk of collateral damage and whether you accept that yes or no, that's a very high strategic level decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last sentence of section 4 a you state: "Artillery assets can only be used in case the safe distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties." Now I'd like you to please explain to the Trial Chamber how this requirement is addressed when using artillery in civilian-populated areas. Practically speaking, how does a commander meet this requirement of a safe distance?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in practice we develop for that soldier collateral damage estimates which are given facts to a commander in a field which gives him exactly which measures he has to take into account before he starts using either artillery, either close air support, either precisions guided munitions or other means that you have available. And as we discussed yesterday, artillery weapon systems combined with regular, I will call it, old-fashioned ammunition, so non-guided ammunition, the normal high-explosion round has a certain level of inaccuracy caused by the system, caused by the ammunition that is used which will -- will give you collateral damage. Besides that you have, I may remind you to the fact that -- that artillery projectiles produce thousands of shrapnel that can fly several hundred metres. To give you an example, in the current mission in Afghanistan, we use collateral damage estimate for non-guided artillery ammunition even for the modest guns of 500 metres. That means that when you have designated an enemy target and there are civilians within that distance of 500 metres, you are not allowed to use the regular artillery weapon systems. The only one who is allowed to give permission if the value of that target is so high is Commander Isaf [phoen] himself, which is the highest operational level in Afghanistan. That's a figure from a current operation, and I think that gives an idea how you should handle a round -- targeting military targets inside a civilian area. It's a complex process, with all the factors and even more factors than I provided you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Chamber how this requirement for a safe distance or whether this requirement for a safe distance also applies to mobile targets which may be moving through a civilian-populated area?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any difference, once -- once a target -- the there is no difference in between because when a target moves inside a civilian-populated area, the same distance applies of 500 metres. Let's take the example from Afghanistan but have you to be aware since the target is moving this distance of 500 metres is also moving with the target. And so you get an even more complicated situation with -- with more risk on collateral damage and not knowing the exact effect that you achieve by combatting with artillery, a moving target. It is a complex thing to do that with artillery. It requires very experienced personnel, it requires forward observer that can constantly see the target moving, and it's a complicated procedure. I would not be in favour of combatting a moving target in a populated area, with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to an application of some of these principles we have been discussing to the specific facts of this case. In section 16 of your expert report, Colonel Konings, which appears at page 14 of the English version and page 32 of the B/C/S, there you were asked to comment on some of the orders and reports in this case, and I'd like to go through some of those with you. Now, under section 16 a you quote a portion of General Gotovina's offensive operation order relating to the tasks which are assigned by him to the artillery rocket groups, including: "Putting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac and Gracac under artillery fire?" Now, in the middle of the last paragraph of your report, which appears on page 33 in the B/C/S, you address this particular language ever General Gotovina's order and you state: "This specific part of the orders gives commanders the green light to use the effect of harassment at a maximum by firing randomly into the named cities. Doing so, fear and casualties will occur, infrastructure will be destroyed, the population will be forced to leave, thus prohibiting the enemy troops to execute their mission in a proper way. This means that the civilian population is targeted to force military units to retreat or even to surrender." I'd like you to please explain to the Chamber, Colonel Konings, why exactly you have reached this particular conclusion based on General Gotovina's order to put those towns under artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we have to remind the discussion that we had just before about the use of the process of targeting. When you use that process, you try to come up with the best weapon systems or the best combination between a target and the effect that you want to achieve. Once you have designated the effect that you want to achieve with your military operation or the de-effect then you start thinking about the weapon systems and the means that you have available to use those against enemy targets in order to achieve effects. And what you see in the orders that I was presented is that up to a certain level, it is clearly described how the artillery support in that operation should be used, where it says against enemy front line, command post, communications, artillery firing positions, up so far that is, to my opinion, normal military explanation of what you want to do with your artillery. I haven't read over -- in the same positions what the effects should be. The effect is it could be neutralising enemy command post or destroying enemy command post or interdiction of logistical supply. I haven't seen that. But, again, the targets that are named in that specific part of the order are, to my opinion, in itself regular military targets that can be combatted with artillery. But in the same sentence you find the words shelling the town of Knin, and I was asked specifically to look at the town of Knin. Without any further explanation, there is no explanation given, what part of the town should be shelled; what military targets in the town should be shelled; what effect should be achieved. It is just one sentence that gives no further explanation whatsoever. And shelling well, means to my part is firing shells against a city with all the risk that are involved: With collateral damage; killing of people; injuring of people; neutralizing or destroying infrastructure; and I cannot help it, but I have to think about the same situation that I witnessed for five months in Sarajevo where exactly the same happened, where without any military purpose the city was shelled; and, to my opinion, was the only purpose of bringing fear to the people, bringing chaos and bringing disorder, and by doing that forcing the defending troops to surrender. Because when you see that civilian population is in anger, is in chaos, is suffering, military troops around an area may be forced to surrender because they see their relatives, their countrymen being harassed. And missing every single detail, every single effect, what you want to achieve by shelling a town, I cannot help coming to the conclusion that seems to me a quite strange military order facing up in a military operational plan that, for the biggest part, looks like a NATO order, if I would have been writing it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in your opinion, Colonel Konings, would a reasonable commander issue such an order if his intent was to fire only upon military targets within the town specified?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object. Needs some clarification. A reasonable commander under what standard, and what country, what background is he talking about? I need more clarification on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe if Mr. Kehoe wants further clarification on that he is free to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think in order understand the answer of the witness, I think it would be good to know what he understand to be reasonable commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Perhaps first, Colonel Konings, you would give us your opinion as to the standards which a reasonable commander applies in giving orders with respect to artillery.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have been debating the facts around the use of artillery already in the last 30 minutes and yesterday. And we have seen that artillery is not the best means - to say at the least - to combat or to attack a civilian-populated area in the first place, and to destroy or even neutralise a stronger infrastructure. Artillery, we have to remind is at its best on combatting unarmoured targets and personnel. But what we did not talk about so far - I have to bring that up now - is the effect of artillery and mortars and everything that is called fire support is the morale aspect, is the fact that artillery causes well, what you -- what we all know what we call the shell-shock: The psychological effect of artillery, which is beyond every imagination. That's what we have to keep in mind. And that effect is an effect that a commander, and I will -- I had not call it reasonable commander. I think any commander should realise that there is always a large psychological factor when you use these type of weapon systems. And especially against civilian population that are not protected, that have no clue whatsoever what is happening around them, and here falling rounds close to the house far away, one hour, one hour at a time, two hours, three hours, 24 hours, that is devastating to go an un-- to a civilian population. And a military commander should that bear in mind always and should try to minimise the risk against a civilian population at the first place. For that reason, you should aim as a commander, using your military force against military targets. And once civilian targets are in the environment, in the direct environment, there is only one thing to do, I think is to act in a proportionate way which means that you have to avoid inflicting damage to a civilian population and civilian infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Konings, the answers that you have been giving here today to my questions and to the questions I put to yesterday and indeed the principles which underlie the expert report and the addendum which you have submitted, are these done under the standards of NATO or of a particular country or of several particular countries? Perhaps you could enlighten the Trial Chamber as to that.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they are coming, of course, from the fact I am an officer of the Royal Netherlands Army. I am educated and trained in the Netherlands. So my most normal, my most important standard, in thinking about these things and in writing them down in our doctrine is the Dutch way, the Netherlands way of thinking, in describing things that. It is, first of all, the most important thing. But being a small country inside NATO, we rely in a quite heavy way on those aspects that are described and are discussed and are done in NATO; so I can give you my answer that my background in dealing with these aspects, and the way I think about these aspects, and the way it is reflects also in our current doctrine is a combination of first of all my Netherlands background; and secondly our involvement in NATO and my experience in dealing with various NATO working groups and writing teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If the Court is satisfied, Your Honour, I will proceed with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now given the standards which you have discussed here in your opinion, Colonel Konings, would a reasonable commander issue an order to put towns under artillery fire if his intent was to fire only upon military targets within those towns?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said before I would clearly expect a very clear, detailed clarification of which targets inside the city of Knin would be the military targets to be fired upon with artillery. The order given now is so generic and can bring so many misunderstanding inside the military chain of command that I never would give that order without any further clarification to my sub-commanders, especially the artillery commanders, but every commander in what to achieve, what effect to achieve inside the city of Knin by using artillery and using the term "shelling the town of Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And again in your opinion, would a reasonable commander leave it to his subordinate commanders to determine how to implement this order without either reviewing or approving what target selections they have made in those particular towns?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, is that a legal standard? If it is, I would like some legal clarification on that. Certainly there is a legal standard to answer that, but if counsel looks like they're eliciting just the opposite, I would like some frame of reference for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again Your Honour I think that is it something that Mr. Kehoe is free to go into on cross-examination simply asking for his opinion as to whether or not a reasonable commander would do as appears to have been done in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking about the opinion. Perhaps you could ask whether usually it's left to and then we heard from this witness how he described a reasonable commander, and a reasonable commander seems to be a mixture of a lot of things. Perhaps some legal matters, perhaps some morale matters. You have asked the question. I can't say that it is -- well, it's clear in its mixed composition of that concept, which might not be able to clarify much further, at the same time, raises still some questions. So perhaps you ask him what is usually done here or there and then whether that is on the basis of what the witness considers to be reasonable command. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, in your experience, is this the type of order which is issued to subordinate commanders without further explanation or specification and simply giving them the authority to implement the order in any way they see fit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just one point of clarification. Pardon me for interrupting, and, Colonel, my apologies. I trust, Your Honour, that Your Honour is looks for his experience and not in fact a legal conclusion. So I trust that was what the Chamber was referring to on lines 18 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think the question is asking for experience. Yes. And so therefore to some extent this interruption was unnecessary and let's try to refrain when it's not necessary to intervene. Mr. Russo, perhaps you repeat the question so that Mr. Konings is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'll simply read my question back to you, Colonel Konings: In your experience, is this type of order, the order to put towns under artillery fire, is this type of order issued to subordinate commanders without further explanation or specification and simply giving them the authority to implement such an order in any way they see fit?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my background and my experience and as we've said before, as I explained to you before, I'm first of all a member of the Netherlands armed forces; and secondly, we operate very close to many NATO forces. I would say it is not appropriate and not done to issue such an order with any further explanation and not leave it to the lower-ranking commanders. Not -- neither to artillery commander, neither to lower brigade commanders or any commander in the chain of command. This type of order would need such level of clarification that no misunderstanding can be done and at least it needs mentioning or explanation of rules of engagement which military targets can be attacked inside a city; what are the effects that you want to achieve with such targets, if it has to be done with artillery. And commanders in the chain of command have to be clear that everything has done to chose the appropriate mean to attack such a military target inside a civilian area because I cannot stop repeating the fact that artillery is maybe the worse system to use inside a civilian-populated area. And it should be very well thought over balance, between the value of that target and the disproportionate use of artillery and the amount of collateral damage that you achieve once using artillery inside a civilian-populated area. So to summarize my answer, it is maybe a bit long, but it is a complicated question, so to summarize my answer, in Netherlands case, or NATO case, this type order would need lots of clarification and would never be given in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to take a look at how General Gotovina's order was passed down, and then I will ask you for some comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please, Mr. Registrar, have Exhibit D970.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now the document on your screen, Colonel Konings, is the attachment for artillery to General Gotovina's order. It is drafted by the general's chief of artillery and looking at the middle of the first page, under section 1 B, it directs the formation of artillery and rocket artillery groups in three different operational groups. Now, if we could please move to page 3, under section 3, which is also the same page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, that order says five different operational groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In any event, page 3 you can see that it directs the artillery and rocket artillery groups to engage in certain specific actions and then directs them to: "Shell the towns of Knin -- of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could please have a look at 65 ter 2210 -- I'm sorry, 2211.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, this is an order for attack for one of the operational groups ordered to be formed in the previous order, and this is the order for attack for the operational group Zadar. Which was supported by artillery group TS-5. Now if we can move to page 8 of this order, and that appears in B/C/S on page 4. And can you see again here, Colonel Konings, where the tasks for the artillery group are laid out and can you again see certain specific instructions they're given and then an order to: "Lay down fire on the towns of Benkovac and Obrovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could finally have Exhibit P1201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could you give the 65 ter number because the Registry has difficulties in uploading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure. That's 65 ter 2209.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, this is the attachment for artillery to the operational group Zadar order for attack, which we have just seen; and it is drafted by the OG Zadar, chief of artillery. And if we move to section 3, which is towards the bottom of page 3 in the English and bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S, you will see there, and moving through that there actually to the next page in the English, you'll see here specific tasks for the artillery and then another order to: "Put the following towns under artillery fire, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac." So, what we have, Colonel Konings, General Gotovina's order at the level of the Split Military District to put certain towns under artillery fire. We see that this same order is then passed down through his chief of artillery to the artillery and artillery rocket groups in the operational groups. And we've seen the operational group order with the same order to put towns under fire, again, passed down through their artillery units without further clarification or explanation or specification?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask the leading to stop. I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have brought the attention to what we see here --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I haven't asked my question yet so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you are describing what you do not see and there is, of course, a certain suggestive effect, at least could be expected. You understand that you are drawing the attention to what is not there, and that is for the witness to find out what is and what isn't there. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just refer him to these texts and say, The orders as written down on paper, then the witness can consider what is there and what is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at the orders as you've seen them here, Colonel Konings, I would like you to please comment for the Chamber on the nature of these orders and explain whether you believe that this is consistent with what you would expect to see in orders for artillery operations in civilian-populated areas.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, when you draw up orders and give them to -- in this case, to artillery units, or I prefer to call it fire support units, you have to mention, you have to clarify what effect you want to achieve by using those specific weapon systems on specified targets. So you have to come up with the effects that you want to have. Otherwise, an artillery commander of an artillery units is not able to make his choice about what types of ammunition to use, how many rounds to use, how the order of fire should be, so the effect is crucial. Mentioning the effect, establishing the effect is coming down from the mission which is given to you by the highest commanders and dictates the way that you use your weapon systems. That is not only for artillery, not only for mortars, same counts for the close air support, same counts for the use of every weapon system that have you in your inventory. The same counts, by the way, for the non-lethal use of various systems that we have in our inventory. So I would expect as we see in this order terms like neutralize command post or destroy command post or attack enemy positions, there, there, and there, with this effect, I would require to have specified the terms put a town under fire or shell a town, with which purpose, with which effect. What should be the outcome of the shelling; is there a certain period; what type of ammunition do I need to use; what effect does the overall commander want to achieve by framing his order in this way? That's what I'm missing. And I think that's crucial that you state what you want to achieve as you do it with attacking military targets; and if you have the intention to attack certain military targets inside a civilian-populated areas you better say so; you better explain to your lower commanders what you want to achieve there; what is the effect of taking the risk in attacking with artillery military targets in a civilian-populated area; so that everybody is aware what he has to do, what the effect should be, and what the risks involved are. Underlying commanders, lower commanders are obliged to know that. That is what we call mission command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would move for the admission of 65 ter 2211. That was the OG Zadar order for attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P1263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And for the Court's information, I'm not moving 65 ter 2209 because I believe that already has an exhibit number. Now if we could move to, Mr. Registrar, again P1259, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Colonel Konings, if you could refer again to your expert report at section 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, even if you're not asking for a number, it might be good for those who might ever wish to read these transcripts to know the exhibit number because otherwise it takes them quite a while to find it on the basis of the 65 ter number you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, it is my understanding it's 65 ter 2209 has been assigned Exhibit P1201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now section 13 of your expert report appears at page 13 in the English version and page 31 in the B/C/S. And there in section 13 you state: "Uncorrected fire should not be used in civilian-populated areas." I'd also like to you turn to section 8F of your expert report. This appears at page 8 in the English version and page 18 in the B/C/S. Now looking at section 8F there you state: "The use of artillery and mortars against targets in civilian-populated areas without having these targets under observation of a forward observer should not be done, unless the target is beyond the already described collateral damage distance and the exact location is known."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now please have 65 ter 4600.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, this is a report of the 134th Home Guard Regiment which was one of the units participating in Operation Storm and I would like you to look at page 2 and if you like in your binder, this is at tap 10. Now at page 2 the last part of the section, section B which in the B/C/S appears on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sorry, I have two -- it appears I have two B/C/S versions up on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There at the top of the page in English which is at -- appears at the end of section B, you will notice where it states: "In the first few hours we had no support from the Zadar OG except for the shelling of the general area of Benkovac without monitoring and the message at 530 hours of the following contents, 'Is anything following on Benkovac?'" Now, I'll ask you to assume for purposes of this question, Colonel Konings, that Benkovac was a civilian-populated area at the time, and given that, and what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, civilian populated area. If I may, Your Honour. A civilian-populated area with military installations in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that until now the focus of the questions was mainly on targets within areas where a civilian population existed and not to exclude any military target in there. And apart from that, I do not think that the witness has any knowledge about that, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's just assume that civilians were living there but that military targets are not excluded to be present as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, with that assumption, and given what you have read or what have I read to you of this report do you consider the shelling of the general area of Benkovac without monitoring to have been an appropriate or lawful use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we said before, if you assume it is civilian-populated area and in that populated area various military targets are established, I would prefer to know, first of all as a military commander, to know exactly what -- how -- no, I have to state that -- rephrase that. I would like to have the area under observation so that I could see what -- if I achieve the facts that I want to achieve. So if I don't know, have a clue, if I reach the effects that I want to achieve with my weapons systems or with my whole operations, I cannot conclude in going to the next step. So that's the reason that commanders do the utmost to try to see and to monitor, to observe what the -- what the effects are that weapon systems are building in the field; and I would particularly be interested in having an area where a combination is of civilian area was in there with mixed military targets, I would be very interested in having that area under observation knowing what is happening there. So that in case when something goes wrong, when something goes totally out of hand, I'm able to stop anything I'm doing there. So putting an area under shelling without any observation, to me, is an at least an inappropriate thing to do. It's dangerous and can cause a lot of trouble, it can cause a lot of damage to infrastructure and worst of all, people that you don't want to harm at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President. I move for the admission of 65 ter 4600.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P1264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1264 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I would like to move now to the addendum to your expert report and ask to you explain a few areas to the Chamber. Now, your addendum appears at tab 3 in your binder and this is Exhibit P1260 MFI. Now, before getting to my questions, Colonel Konings, I would like you to first explain to the Chamber the methodology that you used to create this addendum. And you touch upon it briefly in section 1 of the addendum itself but I would like you to please explain it to the Chamber, how you approached the task of answering the questions put to you by the OTP, what materials you reviewed, and what assumption you made?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As told by Mr. Russo, I have been given information on the situation in and around Knin. I have approached that information, trying to analyse it in the same way as we do analysing an operation in -- in NATO. I did that, of course, in a simplified form, and the way you do that is you take into account all the facts that are around you, so you try to describe for yourself the whole operating environment. That means you have a look upon all the actors that operate in the environment. I mean by that the enemy or the opponent or the adversary, no matter how you call it. You look to population, you look upon your own forces, you look upon the geography of the area, how is the infrastructure, you look at factors like weather and that kind of stuff. And when you look upon the infrastructure or the area, you also look upon the fact which military targets are in that area, how are they connected to the enemy, and what is their value, do I need to combat them, and if so do I need to do that with artillery, with close air support or with any other means that I have in my inventory. And the last thing I describe is, of course, the targeting process. So building -- I have tried to building my answer to the OTP around that analysis that we do inside a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Now, let's begin with section 2 a 1, on page 1 in the English version and also on page 1 of the B/C/S. And in that section you indicate that an element of your analysis included the fact that Knin was a high-value target and its capture was important to the Croatian army. And you state that this is reflected in the "Op order of the Croatian army." And if we could just very quickly have Exhibit P1125, brought up on the screen, and, Colonel Konings, P1125 is at tab 6 of your binder. Now, can you please have a look at Exhibit P1125 and can you clarify for the Chamber whether this order General Gotovina's offensive operation order is the Op order to which you are referring in the addendum?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the order that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Chamber what you found in this offensive operation order that led to you conclude that Knin was a high-value target?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are various places that Knin is called upon. For example one of the main forces are grouped to work along various axis. One of them is Bosansko Grahovo to Knin, and you can read there that troops working along that axis have to cut off communications leading from Knin, have to encircle Knin, and have to take control of Knin. So that brings me to the conclusion that Knin is seen as a very important city. Cutting off the city and circling the city and taking control of that seems to me to be a high-value target. It is -- its loss of the city is a major blow for the opposite party and taking of the city is a crucial factor in the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in section 2 c of the addendum and if we could move back to that, that's P1260, MFI. Again, at tab 3 of your binder, Colonel Konings. In section 2 c, you detail the list of alleged military objectives which you were asked to consider and comment upon, and you discuss the military value for each and whether under facts assumed in your analysis you considered it to be legitimate to fire artillery at each of the objectives. I would like to take you through some of those objectives and have you briefly explain your position with respect to each. However, I'd first like to take a look at section 2 c i, which is also on page 1 in the English but appears in page 2 on the B/C/S. And there you state: "The list of targets contains a mix of military targets and non-military targets. The majority of the military targets are in the direct environment of civilian populated areas which makes them not acceptable for attack with any indirect fire support means." Now can you please explain for the Chamber why being in the direct environment of a civilian populated area makes a military target not acceptable for attack with artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has in the first place to do with the legality effects that occur when artillery is used. We have discussed yesterday the possibility of a blast and shrapnels, especially shrapnels can fly very far away. And it has to do with the inaccuracy that artillery projectiles have in their basis. That's something that belongs to the ballistic behaviour and you cannot prohibit that in using artillery projectiles. So you have a chance in hitting a target and you have a chance at a certain number of projectiles is not hitting a target and falling in the direct environment of the target. And depending on how dense the buildings around -- the civilian buildings around a military target are, you have the risk of giving of -- of getting collateral damage to property and worse to personnel, to people. And the third thing is what we discussed for the first time today is the psychological effect that you will have throughout a civilian-populated area when using artillery projectiles not only in the close proximity but also further away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you would allow me, I would like to seek clarification on one issue. In your report, Mr. Konings, you give the surface, the area, which is covered by the fragments of 120-millimetre projectiles, 1600 square metres, and even up to 2100 metres, if the projectile explodes at three metres high. You give for 81-millimetre mortars, you give also similar cyphers. Now could you tell us, the largest area covered by an artillery projectile would be -- would that be the 203 millimetres and what area would that cover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have those exact figures available, Your Honour. I have taken the 120 because that is a quite commonly used mortar projectile. I'm quite sure those are for 155 and 203 available, and the area covered by those types of projectiles will be bigger than the 1600 square metres that you describe for 120, but I do not have the exact figures available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if not the exact numbers, could you give us more or less in what size - I have to think - would it be double the surface, would it be triple?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is very hard to guess that. I prefer to say it will be bigger, but I have no figures available; and I didn't study that in the late period in order to find that out, so I cannot be more precise than I say now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any way, perhaps, that during the breaks you find out about and find a source or -- or would you know about a source or would the parties -- could the parties assist me in -- because we now it for 81-millimetre, 120-millimetre but not for the -- for the heavier weapon systems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given some time, I can find it out. I have sources inside the Dutch army that I can rely on. It may take either a day or two to get that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also addressing the parties. Would the parties have information because this usually comes from tables, isn't it, which are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just in the spirit of accuracy, Judge, it is not necessarily square metres. It's radius that is the important effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that, of course, depending on the angle of descent but if we're talking about maximum, that would be if the projectile falls under a 90-degree angle because then it is the widest. It doesn't touch the ground easily, it doesn't have to climb up on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore I take it that there must be tables -- I mean if we know it and the surface, of course, usually at the -- I would say at the ideal landing giving the largest area covered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, there are no ideal circumstances and the fact that you are describing a projectile landing on a 90-degree angle, first of all that will never happen. That's theoretical approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand because then we have to fire just in the air and then it comes down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then it comes down to your own positions. So That doesn't work but the -- the angle of impact, the 1600 square metres is never an exact square. It is just to give you an idea how large that area is. The same we say for the when you use a DPICM - and I know that this is a tricky issue, but I don't mean anything with that - but the coverage of one DPICM emission is as large as a football field. But can you imagine this a shrapnel doesn't stop at the end of the field. So shrapnels fly around, they have a very irregular pattern. Only to give a reader an idea how large an area is that can be covered by a mortar projectile hitting the ground in an average angle of impact, I have given this example of 1600 square metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is then the 1600 square metres is as far as the shrapnel flies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is it as far -- that is the theoretic approach as far as most of the shrapnels fly. It gives you an idea of an area how large it is, but there are, of course, shrapnels that fly further. For that reason, in Afghanistan we take that 500 metres distance to a civilian target because we are then 100 percent sure that no shrapnel of a 155-projectile will fly beyond the distance of 500 metres. That is the reason why we take 500 metres from the point of impact. There must be analysis tables we use tables for analysis of targets which gives you coverage and gives you the numbers of the projectiles that have you to use. I can try to get the tables but that will cause time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason I am asking because I heard several times, I heard you saying several times shrapnel flies hundreds and hundreds of metres. And at the same time, I have some difficulties in reconciling this with the 1600 or the 2100 square metres because that would be -- if it would be a circle, and I do understand it is not a circle, but if it would be a circle that would be radius of far less than 100 metres. So if you say that is where most of the shrapnel flies or lands, then -- I am trying to understand what it actually means because from what I know is a football pitch is already some 5.000 so that would be half a football pitch, approximately, even less, 2100. So, therefore, the 500 metres, the several tens of metres, half a football pitch, I'm trying to understand what it actually means when you say shrapnel flies several hundreds of metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, shrapnel can fly several hundreds of metres. That depends on, first of all, the projectile itself, the way it explodes, the angle of impact; and in a theoretic circumstances where you test exploding -- where you test artillery projectile there have been known measurements. And I know that these measurements are there. And then you can find shrapnels back up to 300 metres. And to be sure that no shrapnel will hit anything else than a military targeting, that is the reason that NATO choses 500 metres distance in Afghanistan related to a 155-projectile. So there are many figures around, but shrapnels can do strange things and can fly very far. They can go up to 2, 300 metres. They have been found during tests - I have seen that in Sarajevo - that they can go beyond that distance and that you find them beyond that distance and they may have capacity to injure people. The 1600 metres, 2100 square metres are more related to the lethal capacity of a projectile. If you are inside a 1600 square metre, you have a fair chance to get killed, but you never can predict how far shrapnels will fly and how the blast of a projectile will work because that is all to do with the place the explosion takes place, the angle of impact, and all circumstances around it. That's -- you cannot predict that and because of this unpredictability, it is the most strongest thing to try to avoid the use of artillery in a civilian-confined area unless you have good reasons to do so because the military target over there has such high value that taking out that target it is acceptable to -- to kill civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now going beyond my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Before we move on, I just wanted to clarify something that you had said to His Honour Judge Orie with respect to the 500 metres distance that you use in NATO, currently uses in NATO, can you clarify whether that distance is used with respect to precision-guided munitions or other kinds of munitions?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That distance is used in relation to non-guided artillery ammunitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to discussing the specific alleged targets that you opined on in your addendum, I would like to show you an interactive aerial photograph that we have of Knin, we're going to be showing this through sanction, Your Honours. This 65 ter 4776.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you'll give us just a moment here to pull this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, do you recognise this aerial photograph of Knin here on your screen?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you make use of a similar photograph in your analysis for the addendum?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I'll just tell you and also inform the Chamber and counsel that the red dots which appear on this photograph are vantage points from which particular photographs were taken, and I trust that there's not going to be any objection with respect to some of the photographs we've shown have been disclosed. I'll be showing some of these throughout the course of this presentation. But, first, let's begin with the northern barracks and for the Chamber's information this is addressed at section 2 c ii of the addendum. In your addendum, Colonel Konings, you identify the northern barracks as a military target and I'd like to you please explain to the Chamber what your assessment was of the value of that as a military target given the information that you were provided?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the information that was given to me said that there would be possible -- a possible presence of a corps HQ and when that is actually a fact that makes it a military target, and I can state that is a valuable military target if the corps headquarter commander is there and has his HQ in a barracks. It is a valuable target. I would estimate it to be there. Besides that, the information given to me was that there were very few other troops in there. No combat troops, no real reserves, only some logistic troops and also the possible presence of the headquarters is also not confirmed or is not stated; so it is very well possible that the headquarters isn't even present. That was the information that was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Chamber why you say in your addendum that it should not have been attacked with artillery on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are numerous reasons that I came to that conclusion. First of all it is -- the barracks are surrounded on various sides by civilian-populated areas, and as I was informed on the first day of the attack, still some 15.000 people were inside the city. Secondly, the barracks contain, the barracks, the buildings on the barracks are rather strong concrete either brick-built building, so the effect of artillery attacking those buildings would be very low unless you use large numbers of artillery projectiles which would even -- which would endanger the environment. And lastly, since are you not sure if the corps commander is there, have you to be sure that he is there and even if he would be in the barracks he would have his headquarters somewhere in one of these buildings. You have to be absolutely sure which building it is, and where he is in that building. You have to know the moment, the place, every single detail; and I assume that he will not have his headquarters on the roof or somewhere close to the roof or in the ceiling. He will have his headquarters somewhere in a protected area, in a basement in a cellar where he is reasonable protected against artillery attacks, having seen those buildings. So that brings a lot of uncertainties against the use of artillery weapon systems for attacking these barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Konings. Now looking at this particular photograph, which is a photograph of one of the buildings there in the barracks, can you give the Chamber some idea of what effect, if any, artillery fire would have on a building like this.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the effect of an artillery projectile on there building, first of all if it hits the building it might -- it will explode. I don't think it will go -- it will even go through the building. It go through the wall. If in case you use a concrete piercing fuse, it will - I guess - I think it will go through, but I'm not quite sure I haven't seen the construction of the buildings myself. But the construction is such that even if the projectiles hit the building it will -- it will take lots of projectile, and I really mean lots, more than hundred to be able to destroy a part of the building. So you can imagine if a HQ is in the lower basement or in the cellar of this building that an artillery shelling of this building will not close down this -- this headquarters in the first place. Projectiles that will miss the building will only leave some marks at the outside or will shatter windows, will blow out a door, et cetera. So it will be superficial damage. It will not be structural which will bring down the building because artillery projectiles in a way that they were used in 1995 are not fit for that unless - what I told you before - you use a lot of projectiles then you are able to bring down a part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now looking at the photo here, can you tell the Court if artillery shells were fired at the building we just looked at what effect that would also have on this building which we see here across the street.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all it depends on the distance that the artillery projectile falls between the two buildings but as we discussed before this distance is such that shrapnels will reach that building that is now on the screen so they will bring damage to that building. They will not destroy the building, but will form a serious danger for people living that are living there in bringing down glass windows, shrapnels that fly into living rooms. People might be on the street and so there will be injuries caused, and in certain cases, people will have the possibility to be -- to be killed. The distance is such that that is capable by doing -- by using high-explosive projectiles. Besides that shelling such a building in the barracks, and I cannot stop saying that, will cause huge psychological effect on the people that are living in those buildings closely in the close environment of the -- of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's move now to the Senjak barracks which is this facility which see here on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could we go back to the previous -- to the northern barracks for a second so --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as to allow us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Would you like that photograph in particular, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to ... Mr. Konings, could you tell us what the distance was between the buildings across the street and the building which may have housed the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it is less than 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now moving to the Senjak barracks, which, again, is this particular facility we see here on the screen. This you address at subsection c iii of your addendum and you also identify the Senjak barracks as a military target, and I would again ask you to explain to the Trial Chamber what you consider to have been the value of that target on the 4th of August, given the information you were provided.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first have to look exactly what -- where the information is on what you gave me. Can you give me a moment? Yeah, have I it here. The Senjak barracks was the information given to me was on rear logistic headquarter with only 40 soldiers manning these facility during artillery attack. So there was some administrative offices, bakery, clothing and food supply. That all in all brings me to the fact that, of course, this is military stuff, military personnel but if you look to the whole of the setting, to the whole of the operation, 40 logistical soldiers cannot bring any -- any direct danger to an attacks forces that wants to attack the city or wants to take control of the city. For that reason, I came to the conclusion it is a military target but of very low value.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you then explain to the Chamber why you indicated that this facility should not have been attacked with artillery on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same as we discussed before. It's surrounded on various sides, up to the north as well, by civilian-populated areas. The information was given to me that 15.000 people were in Knin on that day. So the risk is very serious, that when you start attacking the barracks, that you will inflict damage to the civilian population as well. Besides that, attacking these buildings, first of all the military target to me is a low-valuable target. So taking out of the target doesn't bring anything directly to the success of the operation; and secondly, these are again strong buildings, so if you want to destroy taking out those 40 soldiers in those building you need to gain a lot of artillery ammunition to do that with the risk we described before of injuring, damaging property and people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, if there were trucks carrying logistical supplies or even carrying weapons inside of this facility on the 4th of August would that change your opinion that it should not have been attacked with artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In, itself it changes if these trucks especially with weapons would be available, it would change something in the possible value of the target. But again taking the risk that you tried to take out some trucks inside the barracks with artillery, opposite the fact that you have the risk that you bring a lot of damage to a civilian area would bring me to the conclusion that I would try to -- to see whether these trucks are staying there so that the weapons are not used by any troops at all; and when they are moved, I would try to see that I could attack them on a place where there is -- much less problem maybe outside the city or on an abandoned road where you can try to attack and destroy those moving -- or moving trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is probably a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is it, Mr. Russo. But let me go back again for one minute to the -- to the last photograph. I asked you, Mr. Konings, what would be the distance and you said less than 100 metres. Now, let me -- and you told us that it should not be attacked by artillery. You earlier told us that if you have an air-burst that the area covered by a 120-millimetre mortar projectile, 120-millimetre projectile would be 2.000 square metres. Now just for me to -- if I would therefore be able to hit that building well, let's say, within 40 metres of it so that makes 60 metres remaining for the distance of 100 metres, then if it would be circular, the area covered and it usually will not be circular but -- then I would have to think of 60 metres remaining. 60 metres in a circle surface being a little bit over 10.000 square metres. I would then find for a 120-millimetre projectile, I would -- in order to be -- to effectively injure or kill people, I would need an area far larger, and you said that 2.000 metres was where it would cause -- have a real effect. So not one piece of shrapnel flying exceptionally far, but that's where the real damage is done. Now, for 60 metres as radius, I would have an area of 10.000 metres which is five times the 2.000 metres you said. Could you help me to better understand what the real risk was of persons being injured or killed at that distance, of 60 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, we are now talking very theoretically about the explosion of one projectile. If you would attack those barracks, if you value that as a military target, and if you know the strength of the building, and in case you choose to use artillery for that for combatting the target you would use much more than one projectile. That means automatically that the chance that in the area between the two buildings, the civilian building on the one hand and the HQ at the other hand, more projectiles will falling. So there will be not one explosion. Several projectiles will hit the building. Several will be at the back side of the building at the -- well, away from the civilian building and others will fall between but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you a second. I try to be a very cautious commander; so knowing that civilians will living at the other side of the building, I'm targeting at a distance of 60 or 80 metres in the opposite direction and with the intention to adjust fire, once I have observed where the projectiles landed. Could you include this in your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, of course, a possibility to do, that you keep -- try to keep the artillery fire on the safe side in comparison with the civilian population. But you never can be sure that no rounds will fall further than you -- than your intention is. Besides that, if you keep the artillery fire on the safe side of that building, the effect that you will achieve on that building, I don't know what the effect should be, either neutralisation or destruction, it will be less because the bigger part of the projectile will either -- will not hit the building so the effect that you want to achieve will be less. That is it a possibility. The risk will still be there that some rounds will fly further than your intention is, and I come back to my most important effect that you achieve by targeting those buildings with artillery is the psychological effect because it doesn't -- it doesn't make any -- any difference whether the rounds are falling left, right, plus, minus from this building, the civilians in that area, in a wide area, and I mean a really wide area, even kilometres away will be panicked. They will be caused chaos because you don't know where the rounds are falling, to whom they are addressed, and what is happening; and that may be the most important thing that a commander -- no, I have to rephrase that. That is the most important thing that a commander has to think about in judging whether he should use artillery - yes or no - against the value of a military target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We'll have a break and resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the ARSK HQ which you discuss at subsection c vii of your addendum, that we can find ... that's this facility here in the middle between the top and bottom red dots. Now in your addendum, Colonel Konings, you do not specifically state that you consider this to be a military target. So first I'd ask you to clarify for the Chamber whether you consider the ARSK HQ to be a military target.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think that you can designate that to be a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And based on the information which you were provided, can you explain to the Chamber what your assessment is of the value of that military target on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well in itself, an overall HQ in the Ministry of Defence to me seems to be a high-valuable, high-valid target, high-priority target to call it like that. So in itself, attacking such a target or trying to neutralise or destroy such a target seems to me to be a regular military act to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you then explain why you say that it should not have been attacked by artillery on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it comes back to what we have been discussing before. It is in a very densed built infrastructure area where the possibility of the presence of -- of civilians is very likely. That's not one thing. The other thing is that the building that was showed to me where the HQ and the Ministry of Defence is located seems to me to be a very strongly-built, multi-storage building. So if you want to achieve a certain effect, and I don't know what effect Croatian forces wanted to achieve there, that was not in my information, I think it is highly unlikely or even impossible that you can destroy such a building with the use of artillery, unless you start using maybe more than 100 rounds, and even then I doubt that can you destroy the building. You will have damage. You will have a part of the building being neutralised but seeing the fact that a HQ will not being on the top floor - it's the same discussion that we had before - it will be in a protected area in this building somewhere in the lower floors or even in the basement. So it is just impossible to bring any effect to an important target somewhere headed in this building with the use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And looking at this photograph here of the building and seeing the proximity of the buildings across the street and from your review of the aerial photograph, the buildings around there, can you give the Chamber an idea of the risk that firing artillery projectiles at the HQ, what's the risk that the projectiles themselves will strike the buildings across the street or further down the street?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see on the photograph it's a -- it is not such a wide street. It is it not an alley. It is a distance of well, I estimate that less than at least 50 metres, 40 metres maybe. It's a normal, regular two-lane street with a sidewalk. Projectiles not hitting the HQ but hitting street will be able to produce a lot of casualties or damage to infrastructure, but especially casualties. Because of the fact that if you see that some of the buildings are rather high so the blast will be -- the pressure will be even higher than when you have an explosion more in the open. I have witnessed unfortunately such an effect in Sarajevo where we had more or less the same situation as here where one mortar projectile fell in between two rather high buildings and killed 40 people on the spot and that was just talking about one projectile. So I can imagine -- first of all, I can imagine that this target is a high-value target for any attacking force because it hides a HQ, it hides -- it has in itself a Ministry of Defence, but the likelihood of hitting civilian population and sheer impossibility in bringing structural harm to this type of buildings and their inhabitants bring me to the conclusion that artillery is not the proper thing to use here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, referring back to your expert report and we don't need to bring this up but for reference it's at section 1 c, you state that one of the purposes of artillery support is to: "Disrupt the enemy/opponent command and control system his combat support means and his capacity/ability to execute the operation for a longer period?" Now wouldn't the destruction or neutralisation of this command HQ disrupt the ARSK's command and control system?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that it will influence any compatibilities of the army when highest headquarter is taken out of action. That doesn't matter from which origin that headquarter is, either it is NATO or Netherlands or Croatian. I don't think that doesn't matter. But in the military chain of command, lower headquarters at the beginning of an operation know what they have to do and will be able to operate, to take the operation further. I do not have any insight in the morale affects of destroying any higher headquarter because it is also known that when you take out the highest commander or a high -- a minister or minister president that can have such a morale effect on troops in the field that they stop fighting. That's a possibility. But that differs from situation from situation, that differs from country to country, it can also have the opposite effect: One should take out the highest commander. Troops can be more determined to defend their own case. So that is speculating on an outcome of what were to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, if one or even possibly two shells struck this building, in your opinion, would that disrupt the ARSK's command and control system?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is hard to say. I assume that the bigger part of the RSK facilities building up of the command post will be in a protective part of this building, will not be on the high floor, on the top floor, or on the ceiling. The only thing you might hope to damage, or in any other case, to destroy may be some aerials that can be on a roof which you use for radio communication. But I'm quite sure that such an important headquarters has more means to communicate with its lower commands in the field, that they will not rely on only one system of radio communications. They probably have double communications, make use of land lines of all types of things that you can think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now discuss the RSK telegraph and post office. And this you address at section 2 c 14 of your addendum. And let me just see here. Now, you indicate in your addendum that this is not a military target and should not be attacked with artillery. And in forming that opinion, Colonel Konings, did you consider that the ARSK might potentially have made use of the communication facilities which were in this building?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a thought that crossed my mind. But it's still -- but then it is still my opinion it is from origin a civilian structure, a civilian part of the infrastructure. Post and -- telegraph and post offices are civilian things, are part of the civilian society. So taking them out, first of all, without any presence of military in there or military use is, I think, not the right way to do. I may call, it is attacking a civilian target. Besides that, commanders have to take into account that when you are able to destroy such an infrastructure, you destroy an important piece of the whole society; and you might want to use that infrastructure later on after the operation is finished yourself. When -- not only that is important but when you destroy it, you deny the civilian population in the area once the conflict is over - and we all hope that a conflict finishes somewhere - you destroy a vital piece of infrastructure and that are all things that have you to take into account when you designate something as a target, yes or no. The fact that these facilities may be used by military, to my opinion, doesn't change immediately to a full, valuable military target. Beside that, the area -- it is in an area with normal houses, civilian houses besides it which brings you they are close to each other, absolutely close to each other, as you can see; so it brings a high risk of collateral damage. And as a last point, I doubt that you can bring any level of destruction to this building. You might again be able to damage the aerial that is on the roof, but you -- I doubt that you can destroy there building in such a way that are you not able to uses any land line afterwards you have done the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And judging from the size of the building there, as you can see relative to the cars out in front of it and the proximity as you indicate of the civilian buildings around it, what's the likelihood that you be able to hit this particular building with artillery without any projectiles landing on the buildings next to it or behind it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that is quite impossible. It is depending on -- on the accuracy of your systems that you have. But I think that using the average system in a range of between 105 and 155 that you will have a very large chance that you will -- that will you hit or at least inflict damage to one of the buildings at the left or the right side of the telegraph and telephone building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to the railway communication centre which you address at 2 c 13, and that I believe is in this building here that -- where you can see the cursor moving. I don't have a particular photograph of that. But in any case, would your answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, it will not be easy to know exactly where the cursor was moving, if it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can describe it as the building -- well, the red dot immediately to the south of the main railway station moving to the left as we view the photograph, it's the first building as you cross the street, which is to the left of that red dot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you consider to be south downwards? Which appears not to be the case in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could then try to describe it again but now with the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, from the main railway station moving immediately west, you find are a red dot and from there moving immediately north once you hit the first street the main railway station is the building immediately across that street. And I believe this is the building which was identified as the railway communication centre. I'm sure counsel will correct me if I am wrong. But in any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, would your answers be the same with respect to the use of artillery against this particular building and the communications facilities which may have been inside of it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have anything to add to my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving now to the RSK power distribution centre which you address at 2 c 16. And that is it this facility that we see on the screen. Now can you please explain to the Chamber why you state that this is not a military target and that it should not be attacked with artillery.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
