utterances.text: Well, it is a -- to my opinion in the description that was begin to me it is a purely civilian target. It supplies power for the civilian society, powers for civilian infrastructure. So I don't see any reason to take that out because military installations, military forces will use their own power supplies. They have mobile generators that they can use besides that. If you take out such power station, you might loose for a longer period power supply in that region; and I don't think that's the thing to do and not to decide for a military commander to take that -- that such kind of power supplies out because you deny the civilian population the use of appropriate means to build up their life again. There is no military necessity to take it out, that building out because it is a pure civilian installations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could I ask a few clarifying questions. Now -- and I'm also addressing you to some extent. You said there is no military necessity. Even if there is no military necessity it might bring some advantage even if you might have achieved that advantage in a different way. Another matter you just said, Well, the military will use their own power equipment. Well, let's just assume that that is damaged by other means of attack, and the military are only too happy that they have still got the civilian power supply and can use it, and perhaps in circumstances here where it is not just military in the field but in -- in a civilian environment, that they may easily use that, for example, and I'm referring to one of your previous answers, in relation to the telephone company. You say, Even if it is used by the military well, that wouldn't change anything. Let's just assume that it was -- and the data do not give a lot of information about that, that land lines were still frequently used in this context by the military, and they were using power supply. Now, do you say it is prohibited, or do you say it doesn't bring you sufficient advantage by saying it's not militarily necessary? I'm a bit lost with the criteria used in relation to questions and answers because we are dealing here not with what would have been the best military way of taking Knin. We're dealing here with an indictment brought against three accused for having committed crimes. It's not entirely clear to me at this moment to what extent we're really touching upon what should be our focus, what should be our core attention, and to what extent we're talking about trying to accommodate concerns for psychological inconvenience to civilians. I'm just trying to understand fully what our focus is at this moment. It is not entirely clear to me, Mr. Russo, and it's -- you certainly will understand, Mr. Konings, that we are not here in a military class how to do the best, but we're here because we're having three indicted persons before us who are charged with crimes. So therefore I would very much like to have a focus on that and not to mix up matters, what would be the best way to do it; but we're talking about what was prohibited or what was not prohibited. And if you say it would not make it impossible to use any land line anymore, that's, of course -- if that would be the criteria that all land lines should be destroyed in order to make it an acceptable attack within those means then, of course, I'm a bit lost as far as criteria are concerned. This is perhaps not a question but an attempt to get both questions and answers focussed again on what really matters in this courtroom. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps I can ask a few questions of the witness to lay some foundation for the reason we're approaching it in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, in order to attack a particular target with artillery -- well first, let me ask it another way. Would it be prohibited in your understanding of the laws or customs of war to attack a facility which -- of which no military use is being made?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I don't have that answer. I don't know whether this is prohibited or not prohibited. I am not a legal guy. I try to explain how we in Netherlands and in NATO approach these aspects, the questions you ask me. And there are enough examples, unfortunately, around us where we see that all types of power supplies, power supply stations, or even civilian targets are attacked by military means. But the position that I have to represent here is the fact that we put the civilian population at the first place. Any operation that you do, you do it between the population and you do it for the population. So that means that you try -- your obligation is to inflict as less damage as you can do to any population that is in your area of operation. And for that reason Dutch armed forces and NATO forces have legal advisors in their staff which are exactly aware of what you allowed to do or which you are not allowed to do. In this case, taking this power supply station as an example, I would like to say that all -- no, all the examples, all the targets that we are discussing about is a mixture of partly military use, military precision, military occupation inside a civilian area, no matter what you think about that. A lot of these infrastructure issues that we are talking about are, in itself, meant to be used by civilians, and also after the conflict. And that's the reason that I say when you attack an area and when you attack military targets in itself that is valid; but the value of all the targets in this area, I seriously doubt about, because hardly any target in this area, no, not any target in this area as was described by me by the OTP is of any high value. In the whole city of Knin were less than 500 soldiers. There were no defence lines, there were no prepared positions. There were no combat troops I try to aim at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are these -- are you now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I try to build up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just interrupt you for one second. When you say there were no more than 500 soldiers, are you referring to the facts as they were put to you or do you have any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say in forming your opinion about the, matter we're talking about a city with less than 500 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be very clear, Your Honour, I'm talking about -- I use the information when I say something here, I use the information that the OTP gave me. I studied that information and as we have discussed before, I have been in Knin; but I have not been in Knin on the moment that this all happened. I have been UNMO in Sarajevo but that is a totally different place, and I may have drawn some experience from there. But that is something else. The point I tried to make in explaining what I'm explaining now is that the combination of the low value of those military targets, the fact that the bigger part of those military targets in the civilian-populated area in combination with the fact that -- especially the first day of the attack, 15.000 people were still there make it very likely, very crucial that you consider artillery not to be the most proper means to use in this area because of its ineffectiveness because of its inaccuracy and because of the fact there is no real military value in that area. And when you say assume that this power station would be used by the military, well, I'm not quite sure that -- that there are rules that this is on legal basis that it is then forbidden to destroy, I don't know. That's another consideration that have you to make. If the destruction of that power station, if it would be used by the military, would cause the collapse of a defence force of Knin within a few hours time or within a day's time and which would spare a lot of other misery that would be a good consideration then to destroy that building. Absolutely true. But you have to consider the fact that when you destroy a power supply station, that you destroy, maybe, for a longer period, a power supply that helps a civilian population to recover from a conflict. That's what I tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's move to the traffic roundabout, and this you address at section 2 c 28 of your addendum. Now, can you explain to the Chamber why you say that this traffic roundabout is not acceptable as a target for artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to fall in some repetition. First of all with the information given to me, there is no direct proof there is any military presence on that roundabout but, of course, that roundabout can be used by military troops to cross that. Secondly, it is again in a rather densed populated area, and a roundabout is not too large, so the possibility of when you use artillery against such a roundabout, it is very well present that you hit one of the buildings or that you inflict damage to people around there. Once a roundabout or a traffic junction is used by military forces to cross about that, of course, then it becomes another status because I can understand or I can imagine that that might be the next question. But seeing the circumstances, that roundabout, I would not choose that roundabout when troops are crossing there to use artillery to try to achieve destruction of troops that are moving around that -- using that roundabout because of the possibility that you inflict damage, severe damage to people that are living around that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, where exactly is the roundabout we are talking about? Could we zoom out a tiny little bit so that we know exactly. Where's -- I expect a circle in a roundabout.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. It's this area that I'm moving the cursor over. I don't know is the Court wants me to again give some reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing, I hardly see any roads there. But I now see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So if the Court will follow me. This is the main road here, coming across the main railway bridge, crosses the roundabout and proceeds in this direction, and then another road follows this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, can you explain to the Chamber whether there is any military advantage to be gained from firing artillery at a roundabout when enemy forces are not actually present on that roundabout?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you want it achieve in using artillery against a roundabout. If you wanted to take that roundabout completely out so that no military vehicle can use it anymore, that could be the effect that you want to achieve. Then it totally depends on how the surface of the roundabout is built and what type of ammunition you will use. Normal tarmac or concrete on a road will be damaged by an exploding 120- or 155-shell but not in a way that is unusable anymore. Doing, destroying a cross-road or a roundabout by means of artillery, you need a lot of rounds for that to make it absolutely un-surfacible [sic]. Seeing the fact that most military vehicles have four-wheel traction or are tractor vehicles they will possibly be able to pass around. Secondly, in this area, they will find another road to -- to get across the city, so they will detour and will found another road. So destroying or neutralising a roundabout or a junction with artillery well, it belongings to the possibilities but you need a lot of rounds for that. It depends on how the structure of the surface is, and I would be against it because you will need lots of ammunition in this civilian-populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to the Tvik factory, and this you address at subsection c 20. Now, you indicate with respect to the Tvik factory: "Targeting this area with artillery is highly unadvisable and can cause substantial collateral non-proportional damage to the civilian population. Although the production of ammunition could be a reason to do so. However, the information in Annex A seems to describe that hardly any activities were noticed before the attack." First, can you explain to the Chamber why the production of ammunition would be a reason to attack the Tvik with artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an ammunition factory is clearly an important military target depending on what is produced and if it has production on that moment, but a military ammunition factory is a military target. That's -- there is no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if the ammunition -- if this facility was in fact producing ammunition, if that ammunition was not being actively moved out of the facility and sent to enemy troops on the front lines on the 4th of August, can you explain to the Chamber what the military value would be of attacking that facility with artillery?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would ask for foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm putting a hypothetical to the witness which doesn't require foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there is a lot of hypothesis in the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: On top of that the fact, Your Honour, that there has been no evidence that ammunition was being produced. In fact, there has been evidence that nothing was being produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, to the contrary. There is evidence that shortly before this attack -- as a matter of fact in July of 1995, there was a video played - and we will pick it up - of the General for the ARSK walking through, talking about the Tvik factory making military supplies for the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact -- let's not repeat all the evidence we have on the Tvik factory being active, not being active, what producing exactly. And, Mr. Russo, of course, a question that came to my mind and which here again comes to my mind is if there was no transportation of any ammunition produced - let's just assume that, that ammunition was produced there - would that -- perhaps we should ask the witness. Would you have to wait until you see any movement of the production before you would make up your mind as to what to do, or would you say, Well, if I know that there is production of ammunition I'd rather not wait until they drive out with their lorries and bring it to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is of course a consideration that you make, yes. When you talk about every target and especially about an ammunition target in this case, you try to consider all the factors that give you the decision either to attack it now or attack it later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Including that even if there is no transportation at this moment of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Including --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- production, it might be there tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Including you can take it out as a -- in a factor, a head of an operation to make sure that that factory will not produce any projectiles or ammunition anymore. But that depends also, I think, on the fact that what is exact produced there, what are the amounts, what is its destination; and in this case, what is the likelihood of causing such a damage because when you fire at an ammunition factory it might well blow up and then you have a huge fire explosion, projectiles flying around which can cause a lot of damage to the environment. And considering all those factors together, and given the fact to me by the OTP that there was no production and no transportation visible and seeing the proportions of the whole operation, I said, Well, then since it is in the civilian environment, it is an unadvisable to attack that area with artillery because you might have secondary explosion. You might cause a lot of extra damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Moving now to the main railway station and also the main railway yards, and these you address at subsection 2 c 23, can you explain to the Chamber why you say that these should not have been attacked with artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we keep focussing, of course, on artillery. But I come back to my fact that this type of displacement railroads is in itself a civilian installations. It is -- that's the first things. So if you destroy this and destruction of such an emplacement needs a lot of ammunition from one time or the other, if you destroy it, it is not serviceable anymore for nobody, not for yourself and not for anybody after the operation. So that is a fact that have you to consider once you decide to attack such an emplacement, yes, and no. Besides that, when you start using artillery against such an emplacement you will need a lots of ammunition to take that emplacement out of action unless you focus on certain choke points where tracks are coming together, where you can more easy take that out. But then are you talking about firing at a point target which artillery is not the most -- easy thing to use. I'm not saying that it is impossible to attack these emplacements with artillery, but I do think that it is very hard to bring any level of destruction that you might need and take out civilian installations that might be used by either yourself or by others later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now move to the ARSK mortar section. And this you address at subsection c 5, and that was indicated to you as having been located at the school which we see here. Now, you state that targeting this mortar platoon with artillery is a possibility but would not be a high priority, and suppression would be the best effect to be achieved. First, can you explain why you say that attacking this mortar platoon with artillery would not be a high priority?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a mortar platoon in itself is a very small target and mortars operate a few metres from each other. So it is -- can be considered to my opinion to be a point target, and point targets in itself are not the ideal suited to be combated with artillery. It is like shooting on a fly with a rifle. Secondly, mortars when they are fired upon, they are light. They are -- they can be very easy pack up and move to another place, so if you do not take them out of action with the first rounds, they will displace and go somewhere else and do their work again. Thirdly, one mortar platoon or one mortar section in the whole context of the operation well, being a commander of a brigade or a task force, I would not really worry about that one mortar section and not use my artillery to try to take them out off action because my artillery are valuable assets. I need them for other things, for the whole of the operation. So I cannot see the real value of one mortar section in this moment I have over a whole operation. I could imagine if on that location was a full-sized artillery battalion located that would be another thing but not a section of mortars of 81-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now moving to the southern army barracks, and this you discuss at section c 4 of your addendum. And that's actually located on this -- in this area. Now, you identify this as one of the few acceptable military targets, and I'll ask you to explain to the Chamber why.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through information given to me and the picture it seems to be in a forested area without the direct presence of civilians, so that's one of the few areas that you could target with artillery. Having not seen the infrastructure itself, how the buildings are taken, how they are built: Is it brick? Is it concrete? And when that's the case, I come back to what I said. If you want to destroy troops inside barracks, inside buildings, artillery not most appropriate means. But all the other factors here make it a more appropriate artillery target than all the others that we discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And given the information that you were provided regarding what this facility was being used for, can you give the Chamber your opinion about what the value would be of attacking this particular facility with artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information given to me is that it was a storage facility for small-arms, medication, and clothing with only five soldiers manning this facility during the attack which brings me to the fact that well, again this is a target that would not bring anything extra to any form of defence of the city of Knin; and being a commander of an attacking force, I would not really worry about the possibilities that those five soldier would have on the effect of my own operation. And for that reason I would not use my artillery, my scarce and very valuable artillery in trying to take out some of the -- the points of that -- of that barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, considering, Colonel Konings, I'll ask you to consider that the remainder of the facility was in fact being used by UN forces on the day of the attack and ask you whether and how that would factor into your calculation about whether or not it was appropriate to fire artillery at that storage facility.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a very hard question for me to answer because I'm not quite sure the way UN forces were looked upon as officially they were peacekeeping forces, but unfortunately my own experience is that we were never looked upon as that. So I don't think I can give a proper answer on that, putting myself in a position. The presence of the UN forces should have been enough not -- should have been enough not to use artillery on that facility because the UN forces were not involved in the conflict and had be looked upon as an independent, impartial force which should not be attacked by or being subject of any artillery attack at all. And using artillery in that area with close proximity of UN forces would have given that risk. But I do think that is a very tricky issue and -- well, let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to the police station which you address at section c 17. Now, can you explain to the Chamber why you say that this is a target of no military value?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information given to me was that there were ten police officers. It might have been that they were militarised, so they were part of the military forces being -- occupying Knin, but I can still see no value, no added value of ten police officers with no addition weapon systems in being able to defend in any way or the other the city of Knin in a proper way. So again I would not bother about those ten soldiers. Again seeing the risk that using artillery against such a facility will cause all the other troubles that we already discussed several times before. So it is hardly any military target. It is -- well, no value for the whole operation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, given -- let me get back to it. Given the location of the police station which is at the red dot here on your screen, given its proximity to the surrounding areas which are civilian-populated areas can you explain to the Court your assessment of the risk of firing artillery at this building what the risk would be to the surrounding civilian population what is the likelihood is that they would be struck by artillery projectiles.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can, of course, not predict the exact likelihood. But as we discussed before the likelihood if -- is there that you will -- that you will inflict damage on civilian personnel in that area. And that depends totally on the effect that you want to achieve in either destroying the whole police station or neutralising because that dictates the number of rounds that you start using. Destroying will mean lots of rounds with a high chance that several of them will fall not on the building but on the populated area and neutralising or another effect will cause -- then you will use less rounds, so the effect in the area around it will be less. So I cannot -- cannot be more precise as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to the RSK president's office and the radio TV and Radio Knin building, and this you address at section c 15 of your addendum. That's the facility in the picture with the tower on top of it. Now you identify this as a high-value target, and I'd like to you explain to the Trial Chamber why it is that you nevertheless state that it should not have been attacked with artillery on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in itself in the description begin to me, it described is the office of the president and his staff. And I can fully imagine that is designated to be a very high-value target because the loss or the taking out of a -- of a president of a nation, a country, may cause -- may bring the effect that -- that -- that a state will collapse or will stop doing things. But again here we have the crucial thing that is a combination of a high-value target in combination with the use of civilian facilities, radio and TV Knin although that can be used for propaganda or that kind of stuff as well. But the point is that the information was given that the president was not present during the attack. So then one main important reason to attack this building, and I'm not saying attack with artillery, one main important reason to attack this building in order to try to take out the president is taken away with the absence of the president. Taking out this building, and in the case the president would be dead, taking out the president with artillery is coming back to the arguments that I used. It is a strong building. The president will not be on the top floor. He will be in a protected area. There is a highly likelihood of hitting of at least damaging civilian properties or civilians; so artillery is not the means to be used here again. Taking out the presidency like that and trying to avoid damage to -- collateral damage needs guided missiles, needs guided artillery projectiles; and guided missiles - I'm not aware whether they were available - guided artillery projectiles were - as far as I know - in 1995 not available, not in any army in the world. So the choice using artillery against this building is not a good one, I think, because you cannot achieve the effect that you want to achieve and have to look for other means if you want to take a president of a country out. If you wanted to do that, but that is a political decision of the parties or the states that are in conflict with each other. I'm not the one who should judge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning to the residential apartment building where the RSK is alleged to have lived and this you address at section c 11. Let me find the area of that. Now, the area being one, I believe, is one of these two apartment complexes. I'm sure counsel will correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe it is this particular one on the end. But in any case, you -- can you explain to the Chamber why you say that this apartment building, even if it contains the president of the RSK, is not acceptable as a target for artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same thing I keep repeating over and over is the fact that it is a combination of factors together. Again it is a strong building. You do not know if the president is present in which location he is; and if is he there, he will probably be not again on the top floor. He will be somewhere else. And seeing that area, seeing that it is a residential apartment you will have the likelihood of -- the high likelihood of inflicting injuries, killings, damage to civilians, and civilian property. But the uncertainty that you are even able to do something about the presence of the president in that area, it is not artillery that you get a certainly that you take a president or one person out in such a building with artillery. You might be able to do it with other means if you accept the risk that you kill civilian people, but artillery even thus giving you a chance in achieving the effect that you want to use. Again for that you need guided weapon systems that cause much less collateral damage, that are much more precise, that can fly through a window or the latest development of precision guided artillery munitions. But as I stated, before they were not available as far as my knowledge is in that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this I would move to admit this particular Knin photo presentation. That's 65 ter 4776.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P1265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd now like to focus on some of the answers that you gave to specific questions put to you by the OTP in the addendum and these appear in section 3 -- section 3 a i appears on page 4 of your addendum on the English version, page 7 of the B/C/S, and the addendum is P1260, MFI. Now in section 3 a i, you address the question of whether a reasonable commander would have engaged in the artillery attack on Knin given the information that you were provided about it and you stated: "The use of artillery seems to be disproportionate especially during the first 90 minutes of the attack. One would expect attacking troops to enter immediate behind this intensive shelling, but the actual seize of the city took place more than 24 hours later." And I'd like you to please explain to the Chamber why you say you would expect the HV troops to have entered Knin immediately behind the initial shelling?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what we call in a military operation preparation fires which are connected to the whole scheme of manoeuvre that you do in an operation. So the purpose of that is you are using artillery and close air support in direct fire weapons that you have is that you try to weaken certain spots in a defence area where you make your own troops able to get through to achieve their goals in the operation. That means that preparation fires need to have a combination, need to have a connection, with what is happening with the rest of the troops of an operation, so as a brigade force, you attack a defence force, a defence area, you do your preparation fire and connect to that, you start manoeuvering and start following that preparation fire in order to achieve your objectives. Because if the period between the preparation fire and the attack is a prolonged one, it might be that the enemy gets the opportunity to move back to its own positions and to re-group and to recreate another defence. So the fact that there is first a rather strong preparation fire during 90 minutes and that nothing happens then that there is an prolonged period of artillery fire with irregular intervals with single shots with some volleys and that even after that the troops enter the city gives me well, the -- the idea that I have written down my addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one clarification there. You were asked by Mr. Russo why you would expect the HV troops to enter the city of Knin immediately after the initial shelling. You started your answer by saying what is what we call preparation fires. So your whole answer is that if the shelling was preparation fire then you would expect the troops to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now what if it was not preparation fire? I mean I'm seeking the basis for your answer because your answer is entirely based on this to be preparation fire. If it was not, what then remains of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my point is that when you look to the structure of what -- what happened in that period and due to the information that was given to me, is that you find a rather structurised first 90 minutes where artillery fire is heavy, a lot shots are used; and that brings me to the conclusion that that could have a preparation fire in order to weaken the defences, the defences, if any, of a city. And when you do that, you expect that enemy attacking troops follow that preparation fire afterwards because otherwise if you don't do that, if you only use artillery then the enemy -- you give the enemy a chance to re-group and to reconstruct the damages that have been done. And then I don't see a reason why you keep up a prolonged artillery attack without any manoeuvre action so far on a city where, due to the information, hardly any troops were available to make any defence. It makes it all strange to me what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, staying with that same answer in section 3 A i, you also state: "With the exception of the shelling of two or three military targets, the use of artillery against the city of Knin is of no direct military essence of limited effectiveness and could have been avoided by entering the city with combat troops from various directions having the information that there would be practically no defence." Now can you clarify for the Chamber what you mean or what you consider to be a lack of defence in the town?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information given to me showed no evidence of any prepared position of roadblocks, of defence lines around or in the city, so I purely base my assumption on what was given by the OTP. Also the fact that the numbers and qualifications of the soldiers present in the city as I said before the information states about less than 500 soldiers, no combat soldiers, only small groups of logistical soldiers, administrative personnel, some staff personnel. Given that, they are not able to form a defence, a real defence against an attacking force of a certain size. Those military -- those -- those limited value of all the military targets in the city, the fact that artillery is very ineffective against most of targets because they are in strong buildings or a populated area brought me to the conclusion - as I was asked to do by the OTP - that you could have entered the city from various direction with a strong force like the Croatian forces had available, again, presented to me by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And would your opinion about that, Colonel Konings, change if sometime during the 4th of August the evening of the 4th, that is the first day of the shelling ARSK units which were on the front line were re-deployed into the areas around Knin in order to defend the town?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, an operation can change on any moment in time and military commanders have to take that into account. So the whole situation could change indeed that reserve forces were moved in to take positions around Knin to defend the city against the attacking force. I haven't seen any information on that from -- from the OTP, but if that happens, then as a commander of an attacking force you have to take your measures and you have to re-evaluate, re-analyse your plan that. Is it quite sure. That's quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if there were units re-deployed to the areas outside of Knin, would you then consider it appropriate to shell the targets that we've identified inside of the town?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I keep repeating that I don't see any -- any added value of those military targets that were described in the city by the OTP, and not in the first case, not in the -- in the situation that you described to me now. I would rather see then that the positions of the troops that were taking positions in the area around Knin would be attacked by artillery because that is an appropriate thing to do if you have a change of defence position of defence lines then that is the first priority that you start attacking with artillery either to prevent that even defence positions are taken, or once they are taken that you try to destroy them, or at least neutralise them in order that you can keep up your own attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Regarding your statement that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Regarding your statement that combat troops should have been used to take Knin, did you consider the difficulty of close fighting even against a small number of enemy troops in an urban area?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I consider that because operating in urban environment is one of the difficult things to do. Due to the presence of civilians, due to close environments, due to the very difficult circumstances, the other effect that weapon systems have inside cities like I described [indiscernible] all other weapon systems have to be used in another way. You have no long sides, you have short sides, you have very chaotic situations even for trained military; so I fully realise that entering a city is a very tricky thing to do. I'm not saying that you should avoid that and there are cases that have you to do that in order to control that city. But given the fact here and again I base my assumptions on what the OTP presented to me that there were only those very small numbers of RSK troops inside the city, I have no information of strong defence forces, roadblocks, or whatever you can use as defence, and know you can use every house as defence - I'm quite aware of that - and of course those 400 soldiers could have tried to defend the city on certain spots. But if you compare that strength, their strength and if it's not an organised strength against the strength of a mechanized larger unit ever nearly 2.000 people with main battle tanks infantry available then I do think that the possibility is there to enter the city from various sides. And I know that the attacking force had to take the risk in casualties on their own side. But in doing so, you could have avoided a lot of destruction or a lot of the use of artillery fire at -- in preparation of that operation. And that's an assumption that a commander has to make between maximum force protection of his own force and taking casualties in order to end a battle as soon as possible because the military trade is not the most easy one in the world, and taking casualties on your own side belongs to that. And that is an assumption, a decision that every commander has to take on every moment of an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in section 3 a i you further stated: "The 4th Guards Brigade that had received the order to take control of the city counted around 1900 personnel and can be clarified as a larger combat unit capable of taking control of the city by means of a fast, well coordinated and controlled action. Doing so, collateral damage to civilians and their property could have been minimised as much as possible." You also mentioned in your previous answer that possibly 500 troops in the town of Knin defending against an attacks force of approximately 2.000. I'd like you to explain to the Court where you got the information that the 4th Guards Brigade numbered around 1900 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the information that I was given by OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could, Mr. Registrar, please have 65 ter 4684, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: For your information, this appears at tab 11 of your binder. If we could focus on the lines 1 through 4 in the column on the immediate left-hand side, focus on the rows 1 through 4. Colonel Konings, do you recognise this as the document which you were provided by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is this why you got the information that approximately 1900 troops made up the 4th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would move for the admission of 65 ter 4684.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1266 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Russo, I'm looking at the clock could you find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe this is one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And, Your Honour, before I move on to the next topic, I wanted to make clear to the Chamber because I understand there may be some problems locating the particular areas that we looked at on the last video presentation. But if the Court refers to Exhibit P1261 MFI, these were the terms of reference which were provided to lieutenant-Colonel Konings, including in the annexes to those terms of reference is a map of Knin with each one of the locations identified by number which corresponds to the information in the annex hypothetical to the name of that location and the information provided regarding that particular location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And P1261 MFI is what, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Those were the terms of reference which the OTP provided the hypothetical facts, the maps, and a few artillery orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That's the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, I would now like to review some of the HV artillery documents which you specifically addressed in your addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please have, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 4511.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, you'll recall that this document was a regular report of the TS-4 artillery group, commanded by Captain Bruno Milin. This is a report dated 4th of August at 1300 hours. And for the Chamber's reference, this is addressed in the addendum at section 6 a, which appears in the English on page 6 and B/C/S on page 10. If we could please move to the second page of this order. And focussing on the entry for 0630 hours where it indicates that five projectiles from a 130-millimetre gun were fired at the hospital in Knin. And, Colonel Konings, I'd like you to please tell the Trial Chamber whether you believe this to reflect a lawfully use of artillery against this hospital?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I honestly think I'm convinced you should not use any weapon systems at all against a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber why.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think that that a hospital is a protected civilian installation and should be free of any war combat activities, no matter how you call it, so it should not be used -- no weapon system should be used against a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And supposing, Colonel Konings, for the sake of argument, that there was an enemy tank or an enemy troop position located in the area near the hospital, would that change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you explain why it wouldn't change your opinion.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the destination of that facility is not changed. It is still a protected -- protected civilian installations where wounded people should get comfort and should be treated. The mere fact that an enemy or an opponent places a weapon system and it doesn't matter whether it is a tank or a mortar system in such a proximity of the -- of a hospital, is - to my opinion - also a very illegal act to do that because doing so you deliberately place weapon systems in the vicinity of a protected installation and you can count on the fact or you may recognise the fact that the opposing party will try to take those weapon systems out. As the other party, you may -- have you to realise that when you start using weapon systems against enemy tanks or other system close to a hospital that you are going down a road that you might not want to go because you -- you will have the possibility to inflict damage to this protected facility, so you should not make the same mistake or the same error as your opposing party has made by involving combat systems or weapon systems with a protected civilian area. So you have to find other solutions to take out the tank is that in the vicinity of a hospital, and the fact is also there that -- I know that is a hypothetical question but one tank is not a direct threat for your own operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now if indeed this artillery group had fired at something at or near the hospital, is that something that you would expect to be reflected in an artillery report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would from every fire, from every fire for a fact that an artillery unit does, I do think that -- that commanders need to know what the effect is, so what has been achieved by using an artillery effect for a fire against a certain area. And that doesn't matter to which target you refer. For the purpose of achieving the objectives of an operation, you need to know what effects you have achieved by using artillery because that's essential. If you do not achieve the effect that you want to achieve you might be willing to repeat that effect for fire, or you might be willing to choose another weapon system in order to reach the effect that you want to achieve. So having a report, what effect you have achieved in using artillery against a specific target is essential for a commander to know how his operation is -- whether his operation is successful, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does the lack of any information in this report regarding the effects any of these projectiles indicate to you about what the aim of this firing was?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, this report not only specific talking about the hospital, this report is a summary of timings and number of projectiles and types of artillery pieces used against a certain area or against a target. It doesn't tell me as an artillery man or as a commanding officer not anything. So I can see no added value to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's move to the entry for 0800 hours where it indicated that six projectiles from a 130-millimetre gun were fired at a residential area in Knin. And I'd ask you to please provide the Trial Chamber with your opinion as to whether or not you consider that to a be a lawful use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, it doesn't tell me anything. It just states the fact that there were six rounds fired at a residential area in Knin. There is no effect, there is no result, there is no purpose; so I don't have any information about that. The only fact is that a residential area gives you the information that it might be an area where still civilian people are living, are working, are doing their things, or trying to get away; so the chance is there -- that there is collateral damage done. But this specific document doesn't give me any information on that whatsoever. In the same place, it could have been that some enemy vehicles were in the vicinity of this residential area which triggered the firing of the six projectiles. But I do not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And taking that example, if there were some enemy troops inside of a residential area would you then consider it appropriate to fire artillery into that residential area?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you specifically state inside the residential area that makes it even more impossible to use artillery against it. Deciding on where they were in the residential area, what the construction of the residential area is that are all factors that you need to take into account before you even decide to use artillery or any other weapon system. So it is very difficult to -- to speculate on that kind of information that is now given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's move to the entry for 1220 hours. And this is on the third page in the English and second page in the B/C/S. And the entry for 1220 indicates that eight projectiles from a 130-millimetre gun were fired "at Knin." And I'd like you to comment for the Chamber on whether you think it is lawful to simply fire artillery at a town in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would have -- this is obviously a document that the witness said is counting the amount of projectiles without a targeting system, and I think that that's what the witness said. Counting exactly what they're doing without some -- counsel has some additional information, without that I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness would give a similar comment as to the last question he would have raised the issue where he said residentiary doesn't tell me anything at all. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a more important issue here, Your Honour, which is that there is a translation error. That is not what it says in the original at 1220.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. We have two entries for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's the entry above the one that says the ten projectiles at 1240, which is where we are in the English at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have in the original, I see two entries for 1220.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the second entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the second entry that we are talking about eight projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then I can read what it really says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read it in the original language then we'll hear the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] "At 1220 from T-130, with eight projectiles upon the bridge in Knin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, let me just check one second. Yes. It looks as if there's a translation issue, Mr. Russo. So would you please rephrase your question, rephrase any reference to this entry to bridge in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'll simply ask a different question with respect to the other 1220 entry which appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the four projectile which appears on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No I'm sorry, Your Honour, it is the entry directly above the one Mr. Misetic just read. Yes, in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English it would be the previous page, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the previous page in English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And there, Colonel Konings, you will see that at 1220 hours four projectiles were fired from a T-130 at Kistanje. And, again, I'll simply ask you to comment for the Court or for the Chamber as to whether or not you believe it to be a lawful use of artillery to fire artillery at a town in general.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, taking a -- a town as a general target for artillery without specification of what you want to achieve there and which targets you exactly want to hit, I do think that is not the way of using artillery. Whether that is unlawful or lawful, I do not think I am -- I have the capacity to judge that. I do think that you have the risk that you target -- the high risk that you target civilian property, civilian personnel; and I can recall that that is against the humanitarian law in aiming artillery weapon systems or any weapon systems at unprotected or even at civilian personnel. But I have to say that only the statement that four projectiles were fired at Kistanje doesn't say to me anything as I said before. I do not know the intention. I can imagine that it is it connected with the -- with the statement in the operational order shelling of cities. But that information is it not here, so everything I say further is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That was actually my next question, Colonel Konings, as to whether you can tell the Chamber that the entries that you see in these reports are consistent with your interpretation of General Gotovina's order to put downs under artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no general order to put -- we have seen a line, and, Mr. Russo, I would insist on -- you see that in the last answer of the witness where he is apparently struggling with what it means, he sees on paper because he says, Whether it is lawful or unlawful I do not know. And just two seconds later, he says, Firing is against humanitarian law under those circumstances. So there are two issues, first, what do these entries here exactly tell us from a factual point of view; and if we are able to establish that, then, of course, the next question, whether or not for witness to answer is whether that would be prohibited under international humanitarian law, yes or no. So I haven't seen any order by General Gotovina on paper to shell cities, but I think we have seen three towns mentioned in an order, and we have paid some attention to that. Would you please be very precise in quoting and referring to other texts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could first move this document, 65 ter 4511, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could now please have 65 ter 4512.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, this is a report by the same artillery group, Colonel Konings, and you'll see this is the report which is dated later in time 2000 hours on 4th of August. You'll see an entry -- if we can look on the first page the entry for 1330 hours. And if we could also find there in the B/C/S. And you will see there that it indicates eight projectiles from a T-130 fired at Knin. And I think opposing counsel will agree with me that this is an accurate translation of what appears in the B/C/S. And with respect to that, I'll ask you the same question, whether or not you consider this firing at Knin to be a lawful use of artillery, as you understand international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think I asked Mr. Russo to make a clear distinction between two facts. Perhaps we first would ask do you have any information as to how to understand this entry here that eight projectiles from a T-130 millimetre were fired at Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you before, Your Honour, it is this type of information, doesn't give me any information at all. So it just said there were eight projectiles fired at Knin without telling me where and what has happened. So if they were fired specified against a residential area then it gives me more information, or if it was specified that they were fired against the HQ of the president, it gives me a specification. I cannot say anything on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be no further specifications as what we find here, would you be able to form an opinion about the use of artillery in such a way? But this is hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight projectiles is referring to a rather small target because with eight projectiles especially in an urban environment as I tried to explain before, you cannot reach a large effect. You can reach neutralisation or some interdiction. That is it something that I can try to derive from what I read here. I dont' have any clue - Knin is a large city - so I don't have any clue where these rounds were falling or what the effect was that the appropriate command tried to achieve. It might have been any effect that you can take out of the box of the use of artillery fire. So I don't want to speculate about what -- against which targets those eight projectiles may have been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if just hypothetically if just an order would have been given - how odd it may have been - fire eight projectiles at Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to my opinion, then you get in another area. If you give that hypothetical order then you take willingly and deliberately the risk that those rounds are falling in an area where only civilians are living. So then I will call it, I will classify it as harassing fire with only one effect, psychological effect on the civilian population. The moment you start specifying where these eight rounds should fall then you get there another direction because then you might specify it to attack with military targets inside a city with all the risk that you take and that we have discussed before. But that is a decision that a commander in a force takes and in every force, it might be arranged differently on which level commands are allowed to take these decisions. I tried to explain that in NATO only the highest commander can take that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by way of one clarification, Judge, and I don't know if I misheard what you said with regard to an order at page 80, line 2 and 3; but this is a report and not an order. So I wasn't sure if Your Honour was referring when you used the word order to this document but this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was referring to the hypothetical situation that what we find in this document would be in a similar way be reflected in an order which again is hypothetical entirely. The document in itself doesn't say anything about who ordered, whether it was done by mistake, whether it was -- it doesn't say anything about this. So there is no misunderstanding about that. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, you answered His Honour Judge Orie's question about what an order to simply shell or fire projectiles into a town and you said that you would classify that as harassing fire. Let me ask you if you would consider harassing fire in a town to be lawful under your understanding of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I just may say, Judge, with regard to opinions on the law, I think the witness said that he is not lawyer and has no opinion on what the law is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he has given a few opinions on the law, but he is not a lawyer but what we can ask him whether during his training, whether -- or during his professional experience, whether he ever was formed an opinion about whether that was prohibited or allowed. That -- could we ask him, that's a factual question. I have rephrased the question it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand your question completely, Your Honour. During my education, my training, and my experience formulating an order like you did before like firing eight rounds randomly into a city without specifying anything to my opinion and to the opinion that we have in our army, and our habits is it that we don't, that that's prohibited because you should aim at military targets and not use artillery in the way that we are now discussing because of the collateral damage, et cetera, et cetera, that we discussed before. And I'm not going into the area, whether that is not lawful against any humanitarian law. In our country, in my army, we are teached not to use artillery in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, referring back to your original expert report, we don't need to bring it up. We went through it earlier what you referred to and quoted under section 16 a: "The portion of General Gotovina's offensive operation order directing the artillery to 'put the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac Obrovac and Gracac under artillery fire.'" I would like your opinion as to whether or not what you read in this report that is on the screen and in the previous report whether you believe those to be consistent with your understanding of what has been ordered in the line to put the towns of Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe that is just speculation, Judge, what he believes. We are asking for an expert opinion at this point and that is complete speculation without some support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me just re-read the question carefully. Yes, I think that an opinion about consistency in relation to this doesn't require the kind of expertise the witness brings; and, second, there is a factual shortcoming that the one is part of an order and the other is only a report on fire that was -- artillery that was fired, projectiles that were fired. Mr. Russo, let me just try to understand. If I say firing at Knin or firing at three towns, whether that -- apart from whether it happened whether that -- there is some consistency the consistency being that there are no further specifics, then even without a thorough military training, I could say that the lack of specifics gives a similarity. Is that what you were seeking to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: A bit more specifically, Your Honour. The witness has opined in his expert report that that particular language in his opinion gives the green light to lower commanders to use as he says the effect of harassment at a maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: He has answered Your Honours question with respect to what do these reports seem to indicate to you and he says this seems to be what I would call harassment fire. I'm simply asking him to link that up to his understanding of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, this question and the possible answers in the opinion of this Chamber will not assist it in making determinations it will have to make. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Staying with this particular report if we can move to the entry for 1500 hours where it indicates that 18 projectiles were fired from a T-130 millimetre at the general area of Knin -- actually, if we could move to the next page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, I meant to stay at the first page. I wanted your opinion as to whether or not you consider the use of artillery against the general area of a civilian-populated town to be lawful?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it say anything about a town, Mr. Russo? Does it say -- we know that Knin is not only a town but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: But a civilian-populated area, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A municipality as well. Let's ask the witness whether he -- in reading this, whether it gives him a clue also in view of his knowledge. He apparently has been in Knin. How do you understand this entry; that is, that is that: "In irregular intervals, a total of 18 projectiles were fired from a T-130 millimetre at the general area of Knin."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to be as honest as I can be, and I have been asked by the Court to be that, the word at irregular intervals is already a step towards the fact that I call it harassing fire because when you use artillery against military targets, you do it quite recognisable way like you fire with various guns, various rounds against specific military target. And a total of 18 projectiles against irregular intervals -- on irregular intervals bring me to the feeling, to the idea - and, of course, I do not have the hard proof of that in this case - that this is a random use of artillery against the so-called general area of Knin which can be everything. It's not confined. It can indeed be some forest areas. It can be indeed the military area, but it can be damn-well a civilian area because they are the most in Knin. And by doing so, firing 18 projectiles in irregular intervals against an area where we cannot deny that there are a lot of civilians in there, you advocate here the use of artillery in a harassing way. There is no proof of that. It is only a report. I know that, but it is already ordered in the OP order that we discussed in the beginning that the artillery had to put the town of Knin under artillery fire under shelling also there without any specification without any effect, without any objective to be reached by that artillery. And I have to go back to my own experience being six months inside the city of Sarajevo where exactly the same happened. There was no military purpose the only purpose of using artillery in this way was harassing a civilian population with the objective to make them flee, to get them out of the city, or to harass them or to create chaos or whatever you want to achieve. I cannot help it. I have to say it in this clear way because that is the connection that I find in using the word irregular intervals, 18 projectiles in the general area of Knin and then the connection with the OP order that we discussed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to move for the admission of 65 ter 4512.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1268 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time there's a document I'd like to move into evidence across the bar table. I don't believe this is an necessity to show it to the witness. It is a similar report of TS4 artillery group for the following day, 5th of August. And that is 65 ter 4535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I had no notice this was coming across the bar table, but I will take a look at it, and I just reserve if we could MFI it at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It was provided in the list of exhibits to be admitted to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber gave some guidance as how to deal with bar table exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This was also part of the artillery bar table motion, Your Honour. I should have mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case then -- but is then is there any need to tender it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe the Court's guidance was that those documents were denied admission without prejudice and the Court strongly encouraged the Prosecution to bring them in, in the context of a witness, and that's what I'm attempting to do with this document here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say that you have established the context on the basis of the reports of the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can take a look at it, Judge. I mean, I have no knowledge this was coming across the bar table --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have it MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't have a theoretically have a -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have it MFI'd and then we'll hear from you. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P1269 MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually I had a second document which also comes from the artillery bar table document motion to move in at this point, this being the report of OG Sibenik which was the Operational Group to which this particular artillery group belonged and is relevant to the damage caused by combat activities if that needs to be MFI'd also that is fine; or I can simply show it to the Court to establish what I believe the relevance to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- if you could provide the Court with hard copies one of these days because -- no, if it is MFI'd, we can find it on our computers as well. But if it is MFI'd, we'll first hear whether there is any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just MFI it, Judge, I could very well have a glance and not have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour, that is 65 ter 4560.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would receive, Mr. Registrar, number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P1270 also marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe and other Defence counsel could we hear from you tomorrow whether there is any objection for 1269 and 1270.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to now have a look at some of the HV target lists. If we could please have 65 ter 6119. And for the Chamber's information, this document is addressed in the addendum at section 6 c which appears at page 7 of the English, page 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Taking a look at this target list, Colonel Konings, you will see that the first target listed is a church in Knin; and I'd like to you please tell the Chamber, given your training and experience, what your opinion is as to whether or not placing a church on a target list is lawful or a lawful use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with my background, it struck me when I saw this first for the first time that you even find a thing like a church on a target list for artillery because a church is a social, cultural, civilian institution that should be looked upon as a no-fire area. So it should not be attacked by any military means if at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, and I I'll let the witness -- answer go. If we have some foundation from the Prosecution as to what church this is and ask the question based on that, given this was HV fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President my question doesn't distinguish between which kind of church, my question is aimed at whether or not any church in the witness's opinion is appropriate to include on a target list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is it your view that independent on any circumstances that putting a church on a target list is, under all circumstances, inappropriate; or I'm hesitant to elicit any legal opinions from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the basic point, the starting point is that you are given the correct status as we look to that, a church should never be on a target list as a starting point. And if a church is on a target list then they are very, very valuable and high ordered reasons to do so. But the basic answer is, a church should not be on a target list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we -- that's a very general statement. No, there was another matter apparently raised. That is, whether this was a HV target list. I'm just looking at the document at this moment. Could you please, Mr. Kehoe, let me just have a look at the document, and it says table of identified targets. Is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any basis for -- you haven't asked the witness so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell the Court that this was a document received by the Office of the Prosecutor from the government of Croatia in response to an a request for assistance for artillery documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And specific target lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From Croatian target lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any further information about it I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is. Is it information which could be discussed -- let's first ask, do you know anything about this target list and this church on this list, or do you have any knowledge about that, Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge specifically about the church that is the matter here, that is listed here. But I have a knowledge about the -- about target lists in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard that you -- your starting point is that churches should not appear on target lists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have heard that. Then I don't think it would be necessary for the witness to ask -- to ask him to leave the courtroom but this document is, although the witness has no specific knowledge about this document, there seems to be some information which might be helpful for the Chamber to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, we heard from that you it was received in response to a request for assistance from the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is some additional information about this for clarity sake that the Chamber, I believe, would want to take into consideration as opposed to a hypothetical discussion that a church and I understand General [sic] Konings is just saying, generally speaking, houses of worship should not be placed under attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is the information about the list that it was a Serb Krajina list which got lost in Croatia, or is it about the church itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is it about the church itself.
